questions.question: What is the difference between debouncing and throttling?
questions.title: Debouncing and throttling
questions.direct_answer: Debouncing waits until calls have stopped for a chosen delay and then runs once, while throttling limits execution to at most once per interval during continued activity. Debounce suits completed intent such as search input; throttle suits periodic progress such as scroll position updates.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the two timing strategies preserve different interaction semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling both approaches delay techniques without a timeline.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Considering edge policy, cancellation, and perceived latency.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Debounce resets its timer after every call.
Throttle permits execution at a limited rate during continued calls.
Debounce suits actions that should follow a pause.
Throttle suits continuous signals that need periodic updates.
Leading and trailing behaviour must be part of the helper's contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Debouncing and throttling both control a frequently called function, but they preserve different user intent. A debounce postpones execution and restarts its wait whenever another call arrives, so a trailing debounce runs after the activity becomes quiet.

For example, a search box can debounce network requests for 250 milliseconds. Typing several characters quickly produces one request for the final text instead of one request per keystroke.

A throttle allows work at a maximum rate while activity continues. A scroll progress indicator may update every 100 milliseconds so the interface remains responsive but still changes during a long scroll. Implementations may run on the leading edge, trailing edge, or both, and that timing is part of their public behaviour.

The delay is a product choice, not a correctness constant. Too much debounce makes controls feel unresponsive, while too little saves little work. Pending timers also need cancellation when a component is removed, and debouncing a request does not prevent an earlier request from returning late; stale-response control is a separate concern.

sections.title: Debounce and throttle event behavior
sections.content: Debounce keeps the final settled intent. Throttle samples progress over time. Their diagrams may look similar, but their guarantees to the user are different.

sections.title: Leading and trailing edges change perceived behaviour
sections.content:
A leading debounce responds immediately and then suppresses calls until quiet; a trailing debounce waits. A throttle can emit immediately and optionally schedule the most recent suppressed call at the trailing edge. Libraries expose these choices because there is no single correct policy.

Timer callbacks run no earlier than their delay and still wait for the event loop. Timing helpers should expose `cancel`, and sometimes `flush`, when lifecycle or testing requires deterministic control.

sections.title: Calls over one activity burst
sections.content:
input:    A─B─C────────D
debounce: ──────C────────D   (after quiet)
throttle: A─────C───────D    (limited rate)

questions.question: How do you prevent stale asynchronous responses from updating the UI?
questions.title: Preventing stale async UI updates
questions.direct_answer: Track which request represents the latest user intent and ignore or abort older work before it commits state. A monotonically increasing request ID can guard the update, while AbortController can also ask fetch to stop. Aborting saves work when supported, but an identity check remains useful at the state boundary.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether asynchronous ordering is modelled as explicit state ownership.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the most recently completed request is the newest one.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combining cooperative cancellation with a guarded commit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Responses can finish in a different order from requests.
Give each request an ID or compare the current query before updating state.
Abort the previous fetch when its result is no longer useful.
Treat AbortError as expected cancellation, not a user-visible failure.
Guard the state commit even when cancellation is available.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A stale-response race happens when user intent changes faster than asynchronous work finishes. Request A starts first, request B starts next, but A returns last and overwrites the newer result.

For example, a user types `java` and then `javascript`. The JavaScript request may finish quickly, render correct results, and then be replaced by the late Java response. Promise callbacks run correctly; the bug is that completion order was mistaken for intent order.

I assign each request a sequence number and update the UI only if its number is still current. For `fetch`, I also abort the previous controller when a new query begins. That can stop network and parsing work, and an abort rejection should be handled as expected cancellation.

Cancellation alone is not a universal guarantee because some operations ignore signals or may already have completed. The final state transition should verify ownership. Loading and error indicators need the same guard so an old request cannot hide the spinner or show an obsolete failure.

sections.title: Async completion order is not intent order
sections.content: The UI needs an explicit rule that says which operation still owns the right to publish state. Time of completion cannot provide that rule.

sections.title: Guard every state written by the operation
sections.content:
A stale operation can update data, loading flags, error text, or pagination metadata. The ownership check belongs around the complete commit, often in one reducer action, rather than only around the main response body.

AbortController is cooperative. `fetch` observes its signal, but a custom promise must be designed to observe cancellation. Even after a fetch response arrives, application processing may continue, so a sequence check remains a cheap final defence.

sections.title: Out-of-order responses
sections.content:
request 1: java       ─────────────► late response ✕ ignored
request 2: javascript     ─────► response ✓ commits
currentRequestId: 1 ─────► 2 ───────────────────────

sections.title: Let only the latest search commit

questions.question: How should client-side form validation be structured?
questions.title: Client-side form validation
questions.direct_answer: Use native input constraints where they express the rule, add JavaScript for cross-field or asynchronous checks, and show errors next to the affected fields with accessible text. Client validation improves feedback but is never a security boundary; the server must validate the same business rules before accepting data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether validation covers usability, accessibility, and server trust.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating client checks as a security control.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Using native constraint APIs before rebuilding them.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use semantic input types and native constraints for simple rules.
Connect error text with aria-describedby and expose invalid state.
Do not erase user input after a failed submission.
Repeat authoritative validation on the server.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Client-side validation should help the user correct data before a request, while the server remains the authority. I begin with semantic HTML such as `type=email`, `required`, and sensible length or numeric constraints because these integrate with browser behaviour and accessibility.

JavaScript adds rules that HTML cannot express cleanly, such as confirming that two password fields match or checking whether a username is available. For example, a submit handler can call `form.checkValidity`, add a field-specific message, focus the first invalid control, and keep all entered values in place.

An error must be more than a red border. The affected control should have a programmatic relationship to readable error text, and the summary or live region should announce changes when appropriate. Validation should run at a helpful time; shouting errors on the first keystroke is usually poor feedback.

Any browser request can be bypassed or changed, so the server repeats type, range, authorization, and business checks. The client then maps structured server errors back to fields without exposing internal exception details.

sections.title: Feedback and trust are separate responsibilities
sections.content: Browser validation shortens the correction loop for a real user. Server validation protects the data and authorization boundary. A complete form flow needs both.

sections.title: Constraint validation already has an API
sections.content:
Controls expose `validity`, `validationMessage`, `checkValidity`, and `reportValidity`. `setCustomValidity` can add a custom rule; clearing it with an empty string is required when the value becomes valid. Disabled controls and some input types do not participate in constraint validation.

Async checks such as username availability are hints until submission, because the result may change before the final request. The server can still reject a name that appeared available a moment earlier.

sections.title: Validation responsibility
sections.content:
input → native constraints → cross-field/async client checks
valid-looking request → server type + business + authorization checks
structured errors → field message + summary → correction

sections.title: Add an accessible cross-field rule
